questions.title: Chemotaxis definition
questions.question: Chemotaxis is:

options.B: Rolling of leukocytes on endothelial surface
options.D: Movement of extravasated neutrophils toward infective agent

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phagocytosis is the recognition, engulfment and killing of a particle once a leukocyte has already reached it — a separate step of leukocyte activation, not the movement that gets the leukocyte there in the first place.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rolling is the loose, tumbling adhesion of leukocytes to activated endothelium, mediated by selectins, and it happens while the leukocyte is still inside the vessel — chemotaxis happens afterwards, once the leukocyte is already in the tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adhesion to endothelium (pavementing) is the firm attachment step mediated by integrins, occurring before emigration — it describes a leukocyte still at the vessel wall, not one already moving through extravascular tissue.
explanations.D: Correct. After extravasating from the blood, leukocytes move toward sites of infection or injury along a chemical gradient — this directed movement is chemotaxis, driven by bacterial products, chemokines, complement C5a and leukotriene B4. This ordered handoff — margination and rolling, then firm adhesion, then emigration, then chemotaxis — is what actually delivers a leukocyte to the site of injury, and chemotaxis is specifically its final, directional step.

questions.learning_objective: Define chemotaxis as the post-extravasation, chemical-gradient-directed movement of leukocytes, distinct from rolling, adhesion and phagocytosis.

questions.title: Macrophage fate after inflammation
questions.question: Which is FALSE about macrophages:

options.B: After the end of inflammation they die and wander off into blood stream

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true, not the FALSE option). Macrophages secrete growth factors — epidermal growth factor, fibroblast growth factor, transforming growth factor beta — that are important in the process of repair, so they genuinely influence healing.
explanations.B: Correct — this is the FALSE statement. Once the initiating stimulus is eliminated and the inflammatory reaction ends, macrophages die or wander off into the lymphatics, not into the blood stream; only in chronic inflammatory sites, where the stimulus persists, does macrophage accumulation continue through ongoing recruitment and local proliferation. The distractor swaps "lymphatics" for "blood stream," which reverses the correct route macrophages actually take once their job is done.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is true, not the FALSE option). Macrophages are derived from blood monocytes, which leave the vessels at the site of inflammation and transform into active, motile, phagocytic macrophages.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is true, not the FALSE option). Macrophages are capable of phagocytosis, although in most acute inflammation they play a lesser phagocytic role than neutrophils until later stages, when they predominate.

questions.learning_objective: State that macrophages die or migrate into the lymphatics, not the blood stream, once an inflammatory stimulus resolves.

questions.title: Diffuse suppurative inflammation example
questions.question: One of the following is an example of diffuse suppurative inflammation:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A carbuncle is multiple communicating deep subcutaneous abscesses opening by multiple sinuses, caused by Staphylococcus aureus's coagulase, which walls the infection off — it is a localized, not diffuse, suppurative pattern.
explanations.B: Correct. Cellulitis is diffuse suppurative inflammation occurring in loose tissues (subcutaneous tissue, orbit, scrotum), commonly caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, whose fibrinolysin dissolves fibrin and lets the infection spread rather than being walled off. Recognising the streptococcal-fibrinolysin mechanism behind cellulitis is what explains why it spreads through tissue planes rather than staying contained like a staphylococcal abscess.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A boil (furuncle) is staphylococcal infection of a hair follicle, walled off by coagulase in the same way as an abscess or carbuncle — a localized, not diffuse, pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An abscess is the defining example of localized suppurative inflammation — a discrete, walled-off collection of pus, the opposite of a spreading, diffuse process.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cellulitis as diffuse (streptococcal fibrinolysin-driven) suppurative inflammation, as opposed to the staphylococcal, coagulase-walled localized forms (abscess, boil, carbuncle).

questions.title: Pseudomembranous inflammation
questions.question: Pseudomembranous inflammation is:

options.A: Mild form of acute suppurative inflammation

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pseudomembranous inflammation is a severe form of acute inflammation of mucous membranes, not mild — a necrotizing toxin kills the surface epithelium outright, which is a more destructive process than ordinary suppuration.
explanations.B: Correct. It is caused by bacteria that produce a powerful necrotizing toxin — diphtheria bacilli in the throat and larynx, and shigella bacilli in the large intestine causing bacillary dysentery — and the mucosa becomes covered by a false membrane of precipitated fibrin, necrotic epithelium and leukocytes. This toxin-driven necrosis of the surface epithelium, not simple pus formation, is what makes pseudomembranous inflammation a severe pattern in its own right.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Involvement of serous cavities (pleura, pericardium, peritoneum) with a fibrin coating giving a 'bread and butter' appearance describes fibrinous inflammation, a different pattern from pseudomembranous inflammation, which affects mucous membranes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyogenic (pus-forming) bacteria such as staphylococci and streptococci cause suppurative inflammation; pseudomembranous inflammation is driven by a specific necrotizing toxin, not simply by pus formation.

questions.learning_objective: State that pseudomembranous inflammation is a severe, toxin-mediated mucosal pattern (diphtheria, bacillary dysentery), not a mild or pyogenic suppurative variant.

questions.title: Granulation tissue
questions.question: Granulation tissue is:

options.B: Occurs during early healing by regeneration
options.D: Formed of fibroblasts and proliferating new capillaries

explanations.A: Incorrect. Avascular scar tissue describes the late, remodelled scar, which granulation tissue matures into — granulation tissue itself is actively vascular, not avascular.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Granulation tissue is the early stage of healing by fibrosis (scar formation), not regeneration — regeneration replaces cells with the same cell type and does not require new granulation tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Granulation tissue is moist, red and bleeds easily, the opposite of pale and dry, which describes the mature scar after remodelling.
explanations.D: Correct. Granulation tissue is formed of proliferated capillaries and fibroblasts (some transformed into myofibroblasts) — the granular appearance of the new capillaries at the base of a healing wound gives the tissue its name. This composition is also why granulation tissue bleeds so readily on contact, a bedside sign clinicians use to recognise it in a healing wound bed.

questions.learning_objective: State that granulation tissue is vascular, moist, red tissue formed of proliferating capillaries and fibroblasts during early healing by fibrosis.

questions.title: Tissues that do not heal by regeneration
questions.question: All of the following can heal by regeneration EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this tissue DOES regenerate, making it not the exception). Hepatocytes are a stable population with strong regenerative capacity — injury confined to the parenchymal cells alone is followed by regeneration and complete restitution.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this tissue DOES regenerate, making it not the exception). Endometrial lining is labile surface epithelium with continuous replicating activity, so it regenerates readily — it is shed and rebuilt every cycle.
explanations.C: Correct. Nerve cells (neurons) are permanent, terminally differentiated cells that are irreversibly post-mitotic in postnatal life — the department book states plainly that neurons do not effectively regenerate, so injury to them results in a scar rather than restitution. This is exactly why central nervous system injury, unlike injury to labile epithelium or bone marrow, always heals by scar rather than by restoring functioning neurons.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this tissue DOES regenerate, making it not the exception). Hematopoietic cells are classic labile tissue with continuous mitotic division, giving them strong regenerative capacity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify neurons as permanent, non-regenerating cells, as opposed to labile (hematopoietic, endometrial) and regeneration-capable stable (hepatocyte) tissue.

questions.title: Liver cirrhosis mechanism
questions.question: In liver healing by fibrosis (liver cirrhosis) occurs if:

options.D: Injury affects liver cells and the framework

explanations.A: Incorrect. Injury confined to the parenchymal (hepatocyte) cells alone is followed by regeneration and complete restitution — the department book states this explicitly as the case that heals without scarring.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Portal tract involvement alone is not the department book's stated cirrhosis mechanism — cirrhosis requires destruction of both the hepatocytes and the surrounding connective-tissue architecture together, not the portal tracts in isolation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The peritoneal (serosal) covering of the liver is not the site the department book names for the cirrhosis mechanism — the relevant structures are the hepatocytes and the internal tissue framework, not the outer covering.
explanations.D: Correct. When chronic injury destroys both the hepatocytes and the connective-tissue architecture — as in chronic hepatitis — the hepatocytes regenerate but fail to reconstruct the original architecture, forming nodules surrounded by fibrous scarring: cirrhosis. This is the mechanistic reason cirrhosis is irreversible once established — the regenerated nodules can restore cell mass but never the original architecture.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that liver cirrhosis results from injury destroying both hepatocytes and the tissue framework together, not hepatocyte injury alone.

questions.title: Chemotactic factors
questions.question: Chemotactic factors include the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Histamine is a vasoactive amine that causes arteriolar dilation and rapidly increases vascular permeability — it is a mediator of the vascular phase of inflammation, not a chemotactic factor that directs leukocyte movement.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Prostaglandins potentiate the effect of histamine and contribute to pain and fever — they are arachidonic acid metabolites with vascular and systemic effects, not chemotactic agents.
explanations.C: Correct. Chemotactic factors named in the department book are bacterial products, chemokines, complement components (particularly C5a), and products of arachidonic acid metabolism (particularly leukotriene B4) — C5a is specifically listed as mediating leukocyte activation, adhesion and chemotaxis. Recognising C5a specifically (rather than histamine or prostaglandins) as chemotactic is what separates the vascular mediators of inflammation from the ones that actually summon leukocytes to the site.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lysosomal enzymes (collagenase, cathepsin) destroy phagocytosed material and can cause tissue damage once released — they act after a leukocyte has already arrived, not as a signal that draws it there.

questions.learning_objective: Name C5a among the chemotactic factors for leukocytes, as distinct from vasoactive/pain mediators (histamine, prostaglandins) and post-arrival digestive enzymes.

questions.title: Cellular events of acute inflammation
questions.question: As regard the cellular events of acute inflammation:

options.A: Neutrophils then monocytes accumulate within the extravascular space
options.B: The adhesion of neutrophils to the vascular endothelium at the sites of acute inflammation is called 'rolling'
options.C: Integrin play a role in margination
options.D: Emigration of leucocytes is followed by leucopenia

explanations.A: Correct. Leukocyte recruitment proceeds neutrophils first, then monocytes, accumulating within the extravascular space — this order (not the reverse) is stated directly in the department book's account of cellular events. Getting this order right also explains why a blood film taken early in acute inflammation is neutrophil-predominant, with monocytes rising only later as the reaction matures.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The firm adhesion of leukocytes to the endothelium is called pavementing, mediated by integrins; rolling is the earlier, loose, tumbling adhesion mediated by selectins — the two terms name different steps, and this option applies the wrong one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Margination is the physical shift of neutrophils out of the axial blood stream into the peripheral plasmatic zone, caused by slowed flow and increased plasma viscosity — it precedes any adhesion molecule engagement; integrins act at the later pavementing (firm adhesion) step, not margination.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Emigration of leukocytes out of the vessel depletes the local marginating pool, not the total circulating white cell count — the systemic response to acute inflammation is typically leukocytosis (driven by cytokine-stimulated colony-stimulating factors), not leucopenia.

questions.learning_objective: Sequence the cellular events of acute inflammation correctly (neutrophils before monocytes; selectins for rolling, integrins for pavementing) and reject the leucopenia distractor.

questions.title: Key cells of chronic inflammation
questions.question: The key cells in chronic inflammation:

explanations.A: This is also textbook-correct (the department book's own formative-assessment answer names lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages together as the chronic-inflammation cell types), but the paper's own printed key marks (c) as the answer, and macrophages are singled out as THE key cell because they drive both the tissue damage and the fibrotic repair that define the chronic picture.
explanations.B: This is also textbook-correct for the same reason as (a) — plasma cells (activated B lymphocytes) are named among the chronic inflammation cell types — but the keyed answer is macrophages specifically, the cell the department book calls 'a key cell in chronic inflammation' in its own dedicated subsection.
explanations.C: Correct. The macrophage is the key cell in chronic inflammation: it is activated by microbial products or T-cell cytokines to proliferate, persist at the site, and secrete both the proteolytic enzymes that cause ongoing tissue damage and the growth factors that drive fibrotic repair. Recognising macrophages as the single defining cell — rather than any one of the several mononuclear types present — is what lets a student distinguish chronic inflammation from the neutrophil-dominated picture of an acute process.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Eosinophils are characteristically found in parasitic infections and IgE-mediated allergic reactions, not as the general key cell of chronic inflammation, which is dominated by macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the macrophage as the key cell of chronic inflammation, distinct from eosinophils, and recognise lymphocytes/plasma cells as fellow mononuclear cells rather than wrong answers.

questions.title: Sinus definition
questions.question: A sinus is:

options.A: A local defect within a surface
options.C: A tract communicating between two surfaces

explanations.A: Incorrect. A local defect within a surface, from separation of inflammatory necrotic tissue, describes an ulcer — a sinus is a tract, not a surface defect.
explanations.B: Correct. A sinus is a blind-ended tract between a deep-seated focus (typically an abscess) and the body surface — for example a peritoneal abscess tracking to the abdominal wall — with exactly one open end. This single-open-end anatomy is exactly why a chronic sinus, unlike a fistula, only ever needs one external opening explored on examination.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A tract communicating between two surfaces or hollow organs is a fistula, which has two open ends, not one — an ano-rectal fistula from a perianal abscess is the worked example.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Overdone repair — excessive fibroblast proliferation and collagen production after dermal injury — describes a keloid, a genetically determined complication unrelated to tract formation.

questions.learning_objective: Define a sinus as a blind-ended tract, distinguishing it from an ulcer (surface defect), a fistula (double-ended tract) and a keloid (overdone repair).

questions.title: PSA tumor marker
questions.question: PSA is a marker of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) is an embryonic tumor of the kidney, not marked by PSA.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma is not tracked by PSA; on immunohistochemistry it is marked instead by cytokeratin, a general carcinoma marker.
explanations.C: Correct. Prostatic specific antigen (PSA) is the department book's named antigen-class tumor marker for cancer of the prostate, used to help detect it and monitor treatment response or recurrence. PSA is elevated by benign prostatic hyperplasia too, which is why it screens for but cannot alone diagnose prostate cancer.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Granulosa cell tumour of the ovary is not the tumor PSA marks; the department book's table assigns PSA specifically to prostate cancer.

questions.learning_objective: Name PSA as the tumor marker for prostatic carcinoma.

questions.title: Aflatoxin and hepatocellular carcinoma
questions.question: Aflatoxins are carcinogen for:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bronchogenic carcinoma is linked instead to aromatic hydrocarbons such as 3,4-benzpyrene in cigarette smoke, not to aflatoxin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Renal cell carcinoma is not the department book's named target of aflatoxin exposure.
explanations.C: Correct. Aflatoxins, produced by the fungus Aspergillus flavus (a food/grain contaminant), cause hepatic (hepatocellular) carcinoma — a distinct chemical route from hepatitis B virus's viral one to the same organ. Aflatoxin exposure is a recognised co-factor with chronic hepatitis B infection in regions where hepatocellular carcinoma incidence is highest.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urothelial (bladder) carcinoma is linked instead to aromatic amines such as beta-naphthylamine, not to aflatoxin.

questions.learning_objective: Name aflatoxin (Aspergillus flavus) as a chemical carcinogen for hepatocellular carcinoma, distinct from other named carcinogen-tumor pairs.

questions.title: Epstein-Barr virus and Burkitt's lymphoma
questions.question: Epstein-Barr virus is a cause the following tumor:

explanations.A: Correct. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is implicated in Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, other B-cell lymphomas, and some Hodgkin's lymphoma. The same virus’s differing tumor associations by geography — Burkitt’s lymphoma in endemic malaria regions, nasopharyngeal carcinoma in parts of East Asia — is a well-recognised teaching point built on this same viral mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lung carcinoma is linked to physical/chemical carcinogens (ionizing radiation, aromatic hydrocarbons), not EBV.
explanations.C: Incorrect. T-cell leukemia/lymphoma is the department book's named tumor for HTLV-1, a different virus from EBV.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Basal cell carcinoma is linked to ultraviolet radiation exposure as a physical carcinogen, not to EBV.

questions.learning_objective: Name Burkitt's lymphoma among the tumors caused by Epstein-Barr virus, distinguishing it from tumors caused by other named carcinogens.

questions.title: Guardian of the genome
questions.question: The following is the guardian of the genome:

explanations.A: Correct. TP53 is the prototypic 'guardian' tumor suppressor gene, sensing genomic damage and arresting the cycle for repair or triggering apoptosis if the damage cannot be repaired; its mutation does not directly transform cells but permits and accelerates further mutation. Because TP53 loss only accelerates further mutation rather than directly transforming a cell, its guardian role is functionally distinct from a governor gene like RB, even though both are tumor suppressors.
explanations.B: Incorrect. RB is a 'governor' tumor suppressor gene, whose product directly stops cell proliferation — a different functional class from the guardian TP53, even though both are tumor suppressors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic gene, not a guardian of the genome — its overexpression (e.g. in follicular lymphoma) prevents cell death rather than sensing DNA damage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. MYC is a proto-oncogene encoding a DNA transcription factor; its amplification drives cancer (e.g. in neuroblastoma) rather than guarding genomic integrity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify TP53 as the guardian of the genome, distinct from the governor tumor suppressor RB and the oncogenes BCL2/MYC.

questions.title: Categories of oncogenes
questions.question: The following are groups of oncogenes EXCEPT:

options.B: Genes which produce the growth factor receptors
options.D: Genes which encode products stop cell proliferation

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS a genuine oncogene category, making it not the exception). Genes producing growth factors are one of the department book's four named oncogene categories.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS a genuine oncogene category, making it not the exception). Genes producing growth factor receptors (e.g. erbB2/HER2) are a named oncogene category.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS a genuine oncogene category, making it not the exception). Genes encoding signal transduction proteins (e.g. RAS) are a named oncogene category.
explanations.D: Correct. Genes whose products stop cell proliferation describe tumor suppressor genes, the functional opposite of oncogenes — an oncogene by definition drives proliferation, so this category cannot belong among the oncogene groups. Every genuine oncogene category instead promotes proliferation in some way — producing a growth factor, its receptor, a signal-transduction protein, or a transcription factor — which is the opposite function from stopping it.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that 'genes that stop proliferation' describes tumor suppressor genes, not one of the four oncogene categories.

questions.title: Disordered proliferation term
questions.question: Disordered proliferation of cells is known as:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Metaplasia is replacement of one mature differentiated cell type by another, not disordered proliferation of a single cell type.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Hyperplasia is increased cell number by division, but the cells remain normally organised and shaped — it is ordered, reversible growth, not disordered proliferation.
explanations.C: Correct. Dysplasia is non-neoplastic disordered proliferation of cells, usually induced by prolonged irritation, and is characterised by loss of normal orderly arrangement (polarity), cellular pleomorphism and nuclear hyperchromasia, and increased mitosis. Dysplasia’s hallmark loss of polarity and increased mitotic activity is also what makes it gradable as low- or high-grade, with high-grade dysplasia sitting immediately before carcinoma in situ.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Atrophy is a decrease in organ size and weight from decreased cell size, the opposite of a proliferative process.

questions.learning_objective: Name dysplasia as disordered, non-neoplastic cellular proliferation with loss of polarity, distinct from metaplasia, hyperplasia and atrophy.

questions.title: Sites of squamous metaplasia
questions.question: Squamous metaplasia does not occur in the following site:

options.B: Gall bladder due to gall stones
options.D: Urinary bladder epithelium in association with Bilharziasis

explanations.A: Incorrect (squamous metaplasia DOES occur here, making it not the exception). In heavy cigarette smokers, the pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium of the bronchi transforms into stratified squamous epithelium, protective but without cilia, so the mucociliary escalator stops working.
explanations.B: Incorrect (squamous metaplasia DOES occur here, making it not the exception). The department book names columnar epithelium of the bile duct and gall bladder undergoing squamous metaplasia due to gall stones as one of its worked examples.
explanations.C: Correct. The lower esophagus undergoes the opposite change: normal squamous epithelium is replaced by columnar epithelium (Barrett's esophagus), which is glandular/intestinal metaplasia, not squamous metaplasia — so this is the site where squamous metaplasia does NOT occur. Recognising this direction of change also explains why Barrett’s esophagus is grouped with intestinal, not squamous, metaplasia in this teaching, even though both are adaptive responses to chronic irritation.
explanations.D: Incorrect (squamous metaplasia DOES occur here, making it not the exception). Transitional bladder epithelium converts to squamous epithelium in the presence of Schistosoma haematobium ova, the same mechanism reused from the Year-1 concept on this metaplasia.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish sites of squamous metaplasia (bronchus, gallbladder, bladder) from Barrett's esophagus, where the metaplastic change runs the opposite direction (squamous to columnar).

questions.title: Malignant cachexia mechanism
questions.question: Which of the following is FALSE about malignant cachexia:

options.A: Marked decrease of body fat and lean body mass
options.C: Cachexia results due to nutritional demands of the tumor
options.D: Cachexia results from action of cytokines produced by tumor and host macrophages

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is true, not the FALSE option). Marked decrease in body fat and lean body mass is a defining feature of cachexia.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is true, not the FALSE option). Marked weakness and anemia accompany the wasting of malignant cachexia.
explanations.C: Correct — this is the FALSE statement. Cachexia does NOT result from the tumor's nutritional demands on the host, even though there is some correlation between tumor size/spread and its severity; the department book states this exclusion explicitly. This distinction matters clinically because feeding a cachectic cancer patient more aggressively does not reverse the wasting, since the process is cytokine-driven rather than a simple calorie deficit.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is true, not the FALSE option). Cachexia results from the action of soluble factors — cytokines such as TNF, produced by both the tumor and host macrophages — acting on host metabolism.

questions.learning_objective: State that malignant cachexia results from cytokine action, not from the tumor's own nutritional demands.

questions.title: Proto-oncogenes definition
questions.question: Normal cellular genes that encode proteins that drive cell proliferation are:

explanations.A: Correct. Proto-oncogenes are normal cellular genes whose products drive cell proliferation — they are present and functioning in every healthy cell, before any mutation. It is only after a gain-of-function change — point mutation, translocation or amplification — that a proto-oncogene becomes the pathological oncogene form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Oncogenes are the mutated, cancer-causing form a proto-oncogene becomes after a gain-of-function change; they are not the normal, unmutated gene.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tumor suppressor genes normally restrain proliferation or sense DNA damage — the functional opposite of driving it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Genes that control apoptosis regulate programmed cell death, a distinct process from proliferation.

questions.learning_objective: Define proto-oncogenes as the normal, unmutated genes driving cell proliferation, distinct from their mutated oncogene form.

questions.title: Histological differentiation of malignant tumors
questions.question: As regard the histological differentiation of malignant tumors:

options.C: Sarcomas may be graded as well differentiated, moderately differentiated, poorly differentiated and undifferentiated
options.D: Better differentiated tumors tend to show great cellular anaplasia and grow faster

explanations.A: Incorrect. Loss of normal polarity (architectural orientation) is a defining feature of anaplasia, not something anaplastic cells retain — this is the reverse of the true relationship.
explanations.B: This statement is also textbook-true — anaplastic cells do show cytologic abnormalities (pleomorphism, hyperchromatism, abnormal mitoses), which is what anaplasia means — but the paper's own printed key marks (c) as the intended answer, and grading by differentiation is the more specific fact this question is built to test.
explanations.C: Correct. Malignant mesenchymal tumors (sarcomas) are, like carcinomas, graded across the same well differentiated / moderately differentiated / poorly differentiated / undifferentiated spectrum, tracking how closely the tumor still resembles its tissue of origin. This grading-by-differentiation principle applies across both major malignant tumor families, giving sarcomas the same four-tier prognostic language pathologists already use for carcinomas.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The relationship runs the opposite way — better-differentiated tumors show LESS cellular anaplasia and grow SLOWER, while undifferentiated tumors show the greatest anaplasia and grow fastest.

questions.learning_objective: State that sarcomas, like carcinomas, are graded across a well-to-undifferentiated spectrum, and recognise that (b) is a true but non-keyed distractor while (a) and (d) invert the real anaplasia-grade relationship.

questions.title: Squamous cell carcinoma immunohistochemistry marker
questions.question: Immunohistochemical study of squamous cell carcinoma show strong expression of which of the following tumor markers:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vimentin is the department book's named immunohistochemical marker for sarcomas (mesenchymal tumors), not carcinomas.
explanations.B: Correct. Cytokeratins (CK) are present in carcinomas — squamous cell carcinoma, an epithelial malignancy, is expected to stain strongly positive for cytokeratin on immunohistochemistry. A cytokeratin-negative, vimentin-positive result on the same specimen would instead point away from carcinoma and toward a sarcoma, which is exactly why this marker pair is used to resolve ambiguous poorly differentiated tumors.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Alpha-fetoprotein is the oncofetal-antigen marker for hepatocellular carcinoma, not for squamous cell carcinoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Calcitonin is the hormone marker for medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, not for squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.learning_objective: Name cytokeratin as the immunohistochemical marker expressed by carcinomas, including squamous cell carcinoma, versus vimentin (sarcomas), AFP (hepatocellular) and calcitonin (medullary thyroid).

questions.title: Hypertrophy definition
questions.question: Hypertrophy is:

options.B: Increase in the size of the cells
options.D: Increase in the number of the cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Disordered, atypical, non-neoplastic cellular proliferation describes dysplasia, not hypertrophy.
explanations.B: Correct. Hypertrophy is increased size and weight of an organ due to increase in the size of its cells, from synthesis and assembly of additional intracellular structural components — without cell division. Because no new cells are made, hypertrophy can only increase organ mass up to the limit of how much each existing cell can enlarge, which is why sustained pathological hypertrophy (e.g. in hypertensive heart disease) eventually fails.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Uncontrolled, autonomous cell growth describes neoplasia, which is irreversible and independent of any ongoing stimulus, unlike hypertrophy, which is reversible and stimulus-dependent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An increase in the number of cells by division describes hyperplasia, the companion adaptation to hypertrophy but mechanistically distinct from it.

questions.learning_objective: Define hypertrophy as increased cell size without division, distinct from hyperplasia (increased cell number), dysplasia and neoplasia.

questions.title: Metaplasia as a precancerous condition
questions.question: Metaplasia may be a precancerous condition in all EXCEPT:

options.A: Squamous metaplasia of the urinary bladder epithelium
options.B: Squamous metaplasia of the bronchial epithelium
options.C: Intestinal metaplasia of the gastric mucosa
options.D: Apocrine metaplasia in fibrocystic disease of the breast

explanations.A: Incorrect (this IS linked to malignancy risk, making it not the exception). Squamous metaplasia of the bladder in bilharziasis is directly named as a site where squamous cell carcinoma develops on top of the metaplastic change.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this IS linked to malignancy risk, making it not the exception). Squamous metaplasia of bronchial epithelium in smokers is associated with squamous cell carcinoma risk.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this IS linked to malignancy risk, making it not the exception). Intestinal metaplasia of the gastric mucosa is one of the named hyperplastic/metaplastic/dysplastic precancerous lesions in the department book's non-hereditary preneoplastic disorders list.
explanations.D: Correct. Apocrine metaplasia in fibrocystic disease of the breast does not carry the same premalignant association in this teaching — of the four sites tested, it is the one the department book's preneoplastic list does not name. This is why apocrine metaplasia in fibrocystic breast disease is generally treated as a benign finding on biopsy, unlike squamous or intestinal metaplasia at the other three sites, which prompt closer surveillance.

questions.learning_objective: Identify apocrine breast metaplasia as not carrying the premalignant association that bladder, bronchial and gastric metaplasia carry in this teaching.

questions.title: Microscopic features of tumors
questions.question: As regard the microscopic Features of tumors:

options.B: Histologic differentiation means the degree of resemblance of the structural pattern of the tumor to that of the normal tissue
options.C: Malignant cells always show low grade (mild) of cellular anaplasia
options.D: All the malignant tumors are well differentiated

explanations.A: Incorrect. Benign tumors are well (perfectly) differentiated, closely mimicking the normal tissue they arose from — the opposite of undifferentiated.
explanations.B: Correct. Histologic differentiation is defined as the degree to which a tumor's structural pattern resembles the normal tissue it arose from — this is the department book's own working definition of the term. This resemblance-to-normal-tissue framing is exactly why a well-differentiated adenocarcinoma still forms recognisable glandular structures, while a poorly differentiated one grows as featureless sheets of cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Malignant cells show grades of anaplasia ranging from mild to marked, not always low grade — grade tracks with aggressiveness across a real range, not a fixed mild level.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Malignant tumors range from well differentiated (grade I) to undifferentiated (grade IV) — they are not all well differentiated, and undifferentiated tumors are in fact the most aggressive.

questions.learning_objective: Define histologic differentiation as structural resemblance to normal tissue, and reject the claims that benign tumors are undifferentiated or that malignant tumors are uniformly low-grade or well differentiated.

questions.title: General features of sarcoma
questions.question: The sarcoma is:

options.D: Mostly large, bulky and expansile mass

explanations.A: Incorrect. A sarcoma is a malignant tumour of mesenchyme (connective tissue, fat, muscle, bone, cartilage and vessels), not of epithelium — a malignant tumour of epithelium is a carcinoma, and the department book's own comparison table sets this definitional pair as the first line of difference between the two.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carcinoma is by far the more common form of malignancy; the book states carcinoma is the most common form of malignancy while sarcoma is much less common, so this option reverses the actual frequency relationship.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sarcomas grow faster than carcinomas, not more slowly — the book's growth-rate row gives carcinoma as rapid and sarcoma as faster than carcinoma, and this greater speed is part of why sarcomas present as large masses before they are found.
explanations.D: Correct. The department book states that most sarcomas form large, bulky, fleshy masses (sarc = flesh in Greek) that are more expansile than carcinomas because of their rapid growth rate, with infiltration mainly at the tumour's edges. Carcinomas, by contrast, are usually less bulky, harder in consistency and show a more irregular infiltrating growth pattern. This size and gross-appearance difference is one of the clearest bedside distinctions the book draws between the two tumour classes, alongside their differing age distribution, spread pattern and microscopic cohesion.

questions.learning_objective: State the general gross features that distinguish a sarcoma from a carcinoma, in particular its large, bulky, expansile size.

questions.title: Causes of edema
questions.question: All the following are causes of edema EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The department book lists increased hydrostatic pressure, not decreased, as a cause of edema: impaired venous return (as in congestive heart failure) or venous obstruction (by thrombus, or external compression such as pregnancy) raises the pressure pushing fluid out of vessels. A fall in hydrostatic pressure would work against fluid leaving the vasculature, so it is the one option among the four that does not belong on the book's causes list.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a true cause, not the EXCEPT). Reduced plasma osmotic pressure — hypoproteinemia from protein-losing glomerulopathies (nephrotic syndrome), liver cirrhosis or malnutrition — is one of the book's five listed causes of edema, because the plasma proteins are what normally pull fluid back into the vessel.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a true cause, not the EXCEPT). Lymphatic obstruction — congenital hypoplasia (Milroy disease), inflammatory lymphadenitis or filariasis, neoplastic permeation, or post-surgical/post-irradiation fibrosis — is one of the book's listed causes, since lymphatics are what drain the excess interstitial fluid that hydrostatic and osmotic forces do not reabsorb.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a true cause, not the EXCEPT). Sodium retention, including from renal hypoperfusion, is one of the book's listed causes of edema — retained sodium retains water with it, expanding the interstitial fluid volume.

questions.learning_objective: List the causes of edema (increased hydrostatic pressure, reduced plasma osmotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, sodium retention, inflammation) and recognise decreased hydrostatic pressure as not one of them.

questions.title: Cause of congestion
questions.question: Congestion is caused by:

options.D: Active vasodilatation of arterioles and capillaries

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increased blood inflow describes hyperemia, an active process due to arteriolar and capillary vasodilatation (as in exercising skeletal muscle or at sites of inflammation), not congestion — the book keeps these two red-tissue conditions apart precisely because one is active (inflow) and the other passive (outflow).
explanations.B: Incorrect. Decreased blood inflow reduces the amount of blood reaching a tissue and tends toward ischemia, not congestion — congestion is about blood that has arrived but cannot leave, so a reduced inflow is not the mechanism the book describes.
explanations.C: Correct. The department book defines congestion as a passive process caused by impaired blood outflow from the tissue, resulting in increased blood content — it may be systemic, as in heart failure, or localized, as with occlusion or external pressure on a vein, and either form may be acute or chronic. This passivity is the key distinction from hyperemia's active vasodilatation, and it is what produces the down-stream findings the book describes in chronic venous congestion of the lung, liver and spleen: distended, blood-engorged organs with, over time, hypoxic injury and fibrosis rather than the simple erythema of hyperemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Active vasodilatation of arterioles and capillaries is the mechanism of hyperemia (physiological, as in exercise, or pathological, as at sites of inflammation), the active counterpart the book explicitly contrasts with the passive process of congestion.

questions.learning_objective: Define congestion as a passive process of impaired venous outflow and distinguish it from the active vasodilatation of hyperemia.

questions.title: Virchow's triad
questions.question: Virchow's triad include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a true element, not the EXCEPT). Endothelial injury is the first, and the book calls it the dominant, element of Virchow's triad — caused by endocarditis, ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques, hemodynamic stress such as hypertension or turbulent flow, or noxious agents such as endotoxin, radiation, hypercholesterolemia or cigarette smoke.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a true element, not the EXCEPT). Alterations in normal blood flow — stasis and turbulence disrupting the normally laminar flow, bringing platelets into contact with the endothelium, preventing dilution of activated clotting factors, retarding the inflow of clotting inhibitors, and promoting endothelial activation — is the book's second element of the triad.
explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The department book names the three elements of Virchow's triad as endothelial injury, alterations in normal blood flow, and hypercoagulability. "Vascular wall injury" is not listed as a separate, distinct member of the triad in the book's own text; it is effectively restating endothelial injury rather than naming a fourth, independent factor, so among the four options it is the one that does not correspond to one of the book's three named elements.
explanations.D: Incorrect (this is a true element, not the EXCEPT). Hypercoagulability — any alteration of the coagulation pathways predisposing to thrombosis, whether heritable (deficiencies of antithrombin III, protein C or protein S) or acquired (oral contraceptives, the hyperestrogenic state of pregnancy, postoperative platelet rises, or procoagulant products released by certain malignancies) — is the book's third element of the triad.

questions.learning_objective: Name the three elements of Virchow's triad (endothelial injury, altered blood flow, hypercoagulability) as the book states them, without inflating the list with a restated fourth term.

questions.title: Major source of pulmonary emboli
questions.question: The major source of pulmonary emboli is:

options.A: Mural thrombi complicating myocardial infarcts of left side of heart
options.C: Thrombi overlying arterial ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques

explanations.A: Incorrect. Left-sided mural thrombi from myocardial infarcts embolize down the systemic arterial tree, not into the pulmonary circulation — the book places them among the sources of systemic embolization, since blood on the left side of the heart flows out to the aorta and its branches, not through the lungs.
explanations.B: Correct. The department book states that most pulmonary emboli come from the deep leg veins, and may also arise from thrombi in the iliac and pelvic veins or the right side of the heart. Venous thrombi almost always occlude the vein and embolize easily, because veins are thin-walled, superficial and therefore easily injured, and blood flow within them is slow — all factors that favour both thrombus formation and its later dislodgement. Because these thromboemboli originate on the venous side, the book's own course-of-emboli rule places their destination in the lungs: emboli from a systemic vein or the right side of the heart impact in the pulmonary circulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thrombi overlying ulcerated arterial atherosclerotic plaques sit on the arterial side of the circulation, so when they embolize they travel downstream in a systemic artery, not to the lungs — the book lists ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques among the sources of systemic, not pulmonary, embolization.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Emboli forming in the portal vein impact in the liver according to the book's own course-of-emboli rule, since portal venous blood drains to the liver rather than to the lungs or a systemic artery.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the deep leg veins as the major source of pulmonary emboli and connect this to the systemic-vein-to-lung course of thromboembolism.

questions.title: Sites of systemic embolism
questions.question: In systemic embolism, the emboli are commonly impacted in:

explanations.A: Correct. The department book lists the lower extremities and the CNS as the common sites of arterial embolization in systemic embolism, with the intestines, kidneys and spleen as less common targets. Systemic emboli mostly originate from the heart (about 80%, chiefly mural thrombi from myocardial infarcts or left atrial thrombosis in conditions such as mitral stenosis), with the remainder from aortic aneurysms, thrombi over ulcerated atherosclerotic plaques, fragmented valvular vegetations, or paradoxical emboli from the venous system. Because these emboli travel out through the aorta and its branches, they lodge in end arteries and typically cause infarction or limb gangrene, and the book specifically names the lower limbs and CNS arteries as the sites where this happens most often.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Systemic emboli travel through arteries, not veins, since they originate on the arterial side of the circulation (from the left heart, aorta, or paradoxically from the venous system through a septal defect) and are then carried onward by arterial flow — CNS veins are not the site the book names for systemic embolic impaction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lung arteries are the destination of pulmonary embolism (emboli arising from a systemic vein or the right side of the heart), which the book treats as the mechanistic opposite of systemic embolism, whose emboli come from the left side of the heart or aorta and lodge in systemic arteries instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lung veins are not a typical site of embolic impaction described by the book for either pulmonary or systemic embolism; pulmonary venous emboli of thrombotic origin would have to bypass the lung's capillary filter altogether, which the book reserves for the special case of very small emboli that reach the pulmonary veins directly, not for the ordinary course of systemic embolism.

questions.learning_objective: State that systemic emboli commonly impact the lower extremities and CNS arteries, and connect this to their arterial (mostly cardiac) origin.

questions.title: Cause of chronic ischemia
questions.question: Chronic ischemia is caused by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A thrombus that occludes an artery does so suddenly and completely, which the book classifies under acute, not chronic, ischemia.
explanations.B: Correct. The department book lists atherosclerosis, along with arteritis (such as marked endarteritis obliterans in syphilis) and artery compression by a tumour, as a cause of chronic ischemia — a gradual, incomplete arterial occlusion, in contrast to the sudden, complete occlusion of acute ischemia. Because the narrowing develops slowly, the tissue has time to develop collaterals; with poor collaterals the outcome is ischemic atrophy and fibrous replacement, as in myocardial fibrosis from coronary atherosclerosis, while good collaterals produce no effect at all. This gradual, progressive narrowing is exactly what distinguishes atherosclerosis mechanistically from the sudden-occlusion causes such as thrombus, embolus or surgical ligature.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An embolus produces a sudden, complete arterial occlusion, which the book classifies as a cause of acute ischemia, not chronic ischemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Surgical ligature of an artery is an abrupt, complete interruption of flow, which the book lists among the causes of acute ischemia rather than the gradual, incomplete narrowing that defines chronic ischemia.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the gradual, incomplete arterial occlusion of chronic ischemia (atherosclerosis, arteritis, compression) from the sudden, complete occlusion of acute ischemia (thrombus, embolus, ligature).

questions.title: Features of dry gangrene
questions.question: Dry Gangrene is characterized by:

options.A: Well-developed line of demarcation & line of separation

explanations.A: Correct. The department book's comparison table gives dry gangrene a well-developed line of demarcation (a red inflammatory zone between gangrenous and viable tissue) and a well-developed line of separation (a groove formed by granulation tissue and fibrosis), which can progress to natural amputation. This is caused by occlusion of arterial blood supply alone — the typical example being senile gangrene of the toes from severe atherosclerosis — so the affected part stays dry, shrunken, mummified and black, with minimal bacterial growth because of the dryness. This sharply defined, slowly extending pattern is exactly what the book contrasts with moist gangrene, whose combined arterial-and-venous occlusion leaves it stuffed with blood and gives it a poorly developed line of demarcation with no natural separation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dry gangrene usually affects exposed limbs (classically the toes and feet), not internal organs; the book assigns internal-organ involvement — as in strangulated hernia, volvulus or intussusception — to moist gangrene instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Putrefaction is slow in dry gangrene precisely because the tissue is dry, which discourages bacterial growth; rapid putrefaction is a feature of moist gangrene, where the blood-stuffed tissue favours putrefactive bacteria.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Toxemia in dry gangrene is mild and not fatal, according to the book's comparison table, because bacterial growth is minimal in the dry tissue; severe, fatal toxemia is the feature the book assigns to moist gangrene, where rapid bacterial putrefaction releases large amounts of toxin.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute a well-developed line of demarcation and line of separation to dry gangrene, and contrast this with the poorly demarcated, toxemic picture of moist gangrene.

questions.title: Site of thrombus propagation
questions.question: Propagation can occur in thrombosis of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Arterial thrombi, such as in the renal artery, generally occlude the artery by adhering tightly to the wall and seldom embolize, and the book's account of propagation — a repeating cycle of clot forming proximal to a tributary, opening opposite it, and the process repeating — is described specifically for a vein that occludes completely, not for an artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The aorta is an exception among arteries in the book's account: thrombi that form there tend to embolize rather than propagate, unlike most arterial thrombi which occlude tightly in place; propagation as the book describes it is a venous phenomenon.
explanations.C: Correct. The department book describes propagation specifically for venous thrombosis: when a thrombus occludes a vein completely, the proximal column of blood clots up to the next tributary, and opposite that tributary — where blood is still moving — another thrombus forms; once this new thrombus also occludes the lumen, the process repeats, producing alternating thrombi and clots that can extend all the way to the heart, which is potentially fatal. Venous thrombi almost always occlude the vein completely (unlike most arterial thrombi, which adhere tightly without necessarily occluding), which is exactly the condition the book's propagation mechanism requires: complete occlusion at one point so blood clots proximally while flow continues past the next tributary. Leg veins are the classic site because thrombosis there is common (thin-walled, superficial, slow flow) and because propagation up the deep venous system is how a calf thrombus can become clinically significant.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vegetations are thrombi that form on cardiac valves, a distinct category in the book's list of sites and types of thrombi; the book's description of propagation is specific to venous thrombosis and is not applied to valvular vegetations.

questions.learning_objective: Explain thrombus propagation as a repeating cycle of complete venous occlusion and new clot formation at the next open tributary, and place it in leg veins rather than arteries or vegetations.

questions.title: Site of mural thrombus
questions.question: Mural thrombus occurs in

explanations.A: Incorrect. The portal vein is not the site the book names for mural thrombi; it is instead a route by which septic thrombophlebitis of GIT venous tributaries can produce portal pyemia, a different process from mural thrombus formation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Capillaries are too small in caliber for the mural thrombi the book describes, which form as layered deposits along the wall of a larger, roomier chamber or vessel; the book's sites for thrombi are the cardiac chambers and aorta (mural), arteries, valves (vegetations) and veins.
explanations.C: Correct. The department book states that mural thrombi form on the walls of the cardiac chambers and the aorta, and, as a rule, do not occlude the lumen — they line the wall of a large space rather than filling a narrow one. This is why mural thrombi are the classic source of systemic emboli in conditions such as myocardial infarction or atrial fibrillation with left atrial dilation: they sit against a chamber wall exposed to fast-moving blood, so fragments readily break free and travel out through the aorta rather than staying fixed as an occlusive plug the way an arterial thrombus does.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Thrombi that occur on cardiac valves are called vegetations in the book's own terminology, a distinct category from mural thrombi, which the book restricts to the cardiac chambers and aorta.

questions.learning_objective: Place mural thrombi in the cardiac chambers and aorta, and distinguish them from valvular vegetations and occlusive arterial or venous thrombi.

questions.title: Cause of pale infarcts
questions.question: Pale infarcts caused by:

options.B: Arterial occlusion in tissues with dual circulations
options.C: Arterial occlusion in previously congested tissues
options.D: Arterial occlusions in solid organs with end-arterial circulations

explanations.A: Incorrect. Venous occlusion is a cause the book lists for red, not pale, infarcts — as in ovarian torsion — because blood trapped upstream of a blocked vein still fills the necrotic zone, giving it a haemorrhagic, red appearance.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The book assigns tissues with dual circulation, such as lung and small intestine, to red infarcts, because the unobstructed parallel supply lets blood flow into the necrotic zone even after the primary vessel is occluded.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Arterial occlusion in a tissue that was already congested is a cause the book lists for red infarcts, since sluggish venous outflow in a previously congested tissue lets blood accumulate in the necrotic area rather than leaving it pale.
explanations.D: Correct. The department book gives arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulations — the heart, spleen and kidney are its named examples — as the cause of pale infarcts. Because there is no parallel or collateral blood supply in an end-arterial organ, once the single supplying artery is blocked no blood can seep into the necrotic zone, so the infarct stays pale rather than becoming blood-tinged. This is the mirror image of the three causes of red infarction the book lists (venous occlusion, dual circulation, or occlusion in a previously congested tissue), all of which share the common thread that blood does manage to re-enter the dead area.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute pale infarcts to arterial occlusion in solid, end-arterial organs (heart, spleen, kidney), and contrast this with the three causes of red infarction.

questions.title: Definition of septicemia
questions.question: The circulation and multiplication of large number of virulent bacteria and their toxins in blood is termed:

explanations.A: Correct. The department book defines septicemia as the circulation of large numbers of multiplying bacteria in the blood stream together with their toxins, usually fatal. It arises either from severe, high-virulence infections (such as meningococcal meningitis) or from an ordinary infection in a host with lowered resistance (such as E. coli, an abscess, or cellulitis), and its manifestations include septic shock, septic inflammation of serous membranes, acute splenic swelling, hemorrhagic necrotic adrenals (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), toxic myocarditis and organ injury, diffuse alveolar damage, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Toxemia is organismal toxins circulating in the blood, without the bacteria themselves necessarily multiplying there in large numbers — the book's own examples (endotoxin from dying gram-negative bacteria, or exotoxins such as tetanus and diphtheria toxin acting at specific sites) are about the toxin's effect, not about bulk bacterial multiplication in the bloodstream.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyaemia is specifically the circulation of septic emboli, originating from septic thrombophlebitis, that impact in small vessels to form pyemic abscesses — a different mechanism from the free multiplication of bacteria in the blood that defines septicemia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bacteraemia is the circulation of low doses or low-virulence organisms in the blood, which the book notes may cause no disease at all except fever, unless there is a pre-existing abnormality such as diseased heart valves — the opposite picture from the large-scale, usually fatal bacterial multiplication that defines septicemia.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish septicemia (multiplying bacteria plus toxins in blood) from bacteraemia, toxemia and pyemia by mechanism.

questions.title: Site of primary tuberculosis
questions.question: The following is a site of primary tuberculosis:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tongue is not among the department book's four listed sites of primary tuberculosis (lungs, intestine, tonsils, skin); it is, however, mentioned separately as a site of tertiary syphilitic gumma, a different disease the exam paper also tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nose is not among the book's listed sites of primary tuberculosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The liver is not among the book's listed sites of primary tuberculosis; hepatic involvement in tuberculosis is instead a feature of hematogenous (miliary) spread once the disease has already been established, not a primary infection site.
explanations.D: Correct. The department book lists the sites of primary tuberculosis as the lungs, intestine, tonsils and skin. Tonsillar infection follows ingestion of the organism, most often via infected unpasteurized milk from a diseased cow in children, producing a primary tonsillar complex of granuloma, tuberculous lymphangitis and cervical lymphadenitis, mirroring the same triad — tuberculous lesion, lymphangitis, lymphadenitis — that defines primary tuberculosis wherever it occurs.

questions.title: Manifestation of primary syphilis
questions.question: The following is a manifestation of primary syphilis:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Mucous patches are a secondary-stage lesion in the department book — skin-rash-like lesions on the mucous membranes of the mouth, pharynx, vagina and anus that may ulcerate into a snail-track pattern — appearing about two months after the primary stage, not at it.
explanations.B: Correct. The department book names the primary stage of syphilis the hard chancre, appearing about two weeks after infection at the site of bacterial entry (genital or extragenital, such as fingers, lip or tongue). It grossly is a single raised red papule that ulcerates within days into a rounded, superficial ulcer with flat edges, a clean floor and firm margin and base, painless yet very infective, healing by a thin atrophic scar, with painless, mobile, separately enlarged draining lymph nodes. Microscopically the covering epithelium is absent and the subepithelial tissue shows syphilitic granulation tissue — dense perivascular plasma cells, lymphocytes and occasional giant cells, with prominent early endarteritis obliterans, the tissue reaction the book treats as syphilis's histological signature at every stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Condyloma latum (broad, bulky skin papules in moist areas such as the axilla or under the breast) is a secondary-stage lesion in the department book, appearing about two months after the primary stage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A generalized skin rash of macules, papules and pustules is a secondary-stage manifestation in the book, appearing about two months after the primary chancre, not at the primary stage itself.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the hard chancre as the primary-stage lesion of syphilis, distinct from the secondary-stage mucous patches, condyloma latum and skin rash.

questions.title: Features of chronic fibrocaseous tuberculosis
questions.question: Chronic fibrocaseous tuberculosis is characterized by the following:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chronic fibrocaseous tuberculosis is a form of secondary pulmonary tuberculosis, occurring in adults from reinfection or reactivation of a dormant primary lesion, not a form of primary tuberculosis.
explanations.B: Correct. The department book describes chronic fibrocaseous pulmonary tuberculosis, which arises with a moderate number of bacilli and moderate immunity, as progressing at the lung apex to an area of caseation surrounded by tuberculous granulation tissue and fibrosis; once caseation involves a bronchus, the caseous material is evacuated and an apical cavity is left, at first yellow and irregular but later smooth from fibrosis, with the fibrous wall progressively destroyed by caseation and reforming further out so the cavity gradually enlarges. Blood vessels and bronchi in the cavity wall are more resistant to caseation than the surrounding lung and so persist as thickened cords or ridges, while the endarteritis affecting them can erode and cause haemoptysis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The book states lymph node lesions are insignificant in chronic fibrocaseous (secondary) tuberculosis, precisely because immunity already developed from the earlier primary infection limits the number of bacilli reaching the nodes inside macrophages — the opposite of what happens in primary tuberculosis, where the tuberculous-lesion/lymphangitis/lymphadenitis triad is prominent.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Acinar lesions do occur in chronic fibrocaseous tuberculosis: part of the caseous material is aspirated into distal bronchioles, producing small clover-leaf-shaped caseating lesions mainly at the lung base, and confluence of these acinar lesions can produce confluent pneumonia.

questions.learning_objective: Describe chronic fibrocaseous (secondary) pulmonary tuberculosis: apical cavitation, insignificant lymph node lesions and acinar lesions from bronchial aspiration.

questions.title: Presentation of primary intestinal tuberculosis
questions.question: Primary intestinal tuberculosis presents mainly by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ulcers with undermined edges — transverse, girdle-shaped ulcers from lymphatic spread along Peyer's patches and solitary follicles — are the book's description of secondary intestinal tuberculosis (from swallowed infected sputum or reactivation), not the primary intestinal complex.
explanations.B: Correct. The department book describes the primary intestinal complex as a small intestinal tubercle forming in Peyer's patches of the terminal ileum, which may coalesce and ulcerate, together with tuberculous lymphangitis and mesenteric draining lymph nodes that become enlarged, caseous and adherent — a finding the book names directly as tabes mesenterica. This mirrors the same tuberculous-lesion/lymphangitis/lymphadenitis pattern the book uses to define primary tuberculosis at every site, with the mesenteric lymphadenitis being the dominant, book-named feature at this one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tuberculous peritonitis is a complication of spread in a patient with low body resistance (progressive primary tuberculosis), not the main presentation of the primary intestinal complex itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intestinal obstruction is a complication the book attributes to fibrosis and stenosis in secondary intestinal tuberculosis, not a main presenting feature of the primary intestinal complex.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the primary intestinal tuberculous complex (terminal ileal tubercle, lymphangitis, tabes mesenterica) and distinguish it from secondary intestinal tuberculosis's girdle ulcers.

questions.title: Features of nodular leprosy
questions.question: Nodular leprosy is characterized by:

explanations.A: Correct. The department book states that in lepromatous (nodular) leprosy, which develops in patients with low TH1 cell-mediated immunity, the granuloma's macrophages engulf Mycobacterium leprae bacilli, which proliferate inside their cytoplasm; the cells become vacuolated and are specifically named lepra cells. This vacuolated-macrophage picture is the book's own histological signature of the lepromatous (nodular) form, in contrast to the epithelioid-cell, non-caseating granuloma the book assigns instead to tuberculoid leprosy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Non-caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid cells, giant cells and lymphocytes are the book's description of tuberculoid leprosy, the high-immunity form, not the nodular (lepromatous) form, whose granuloma is instead built from macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells and giant cells with vacuolated, bacilli-laden lepra cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypopigmented, anesthetic skin macules with impaired sensation are the book's description of tuberculoid leprosy, not nodular leprosy, whose skin lesions are instead multiple nodules that can give a leonine facies.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Nodular (lepromatous) leprosy develops in patients with low, not high, TH1 cell-mediated immunity — the book explicitly attributes the strong, effective TH1/IFN-gamma response, and hence the low bacillary burden, to the tuberculoid form instead.

questions.learning_objective: Attribute vacuolated macrophages (lepra cells) to low-immunity lepromatous (nodular) leprosy, and contrast this with the non-caseating granuloma and anesthetic patches of high-immunity tuberculoid leprosy.

questions.title: Features of actinomycosis
questions.question: Actinomycosis:

options.B: Characterized by the presence of epithelioid granuloma

explanations.A: Incorrect. Actinomycosis is caused by Actinomyces israelii, an anaerobic gram-positive bacterium (a commensal of the mouth, carious teeth and intestine that becomes pathogenic endogenously with lowered immunity), not a fungus, even though its clinical picture of draining sinuses and granules superficially resembles a fungal mycetoma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The book describes each actinomycotic abscess as having three zones — a central zone of pus containing bacterial colonies (sulphur granules), a mid zone of inflammatory cells (polymorphs, pus cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, macrophages and giant cells), and an outer zone of fibrosis — rather than the epithelioid-cell granuloma structure seen in tuberculosis or leprosy.
explanations.C: Correct. The department book describes actinomycosis grossly as multiple intercommunicating abscesses opening to the surface through multiple sinuses, discharging pus and yellow bacterial colonies known as sulphur granules. Cervicofacial actinomycosis (60% of cases, around the angle of the mandible and neck) is the commonest site, entering through the buccal mucosa after minor trauma; intestinal (20%), pulmonary (15%) and skin (5%) forms make up the rest, and because the causative filaments are too large to enter lymphatics, spread when it occurs is by blood rather than lymphatic channels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Actinomycosis runs a chronic course, with the book describing multiple intercommunicating abscesses and sinuses forming over time, not an acute presentation.

questions.learning_objective: Describe actinomycosis as a chronic, gram-positive bacterial disease with multiple sinuses discharging sulphur granules, not a fungal or acute condition.

questions.title: Definition of pyemia
questions.question: Pyemia is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Circulating bacteria and their toxins together describes septicemia, the book's own definition, not pyemia — pyemia's defining feature is the emboli themselves, not free-circulating organisms.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Circulating highly virulent bacteria alone, without emboli, better matches the book's account of the etiology of septicemia (severe infections with high-virulence organisms) rather than the emboli-based definition of pyemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Phlebothrombosis is one cause the book lists for venous thrombosis in general — thrombosis initiated by factors other than inflammation, such as stasis in calf veins of cardiac patients — but it is not itself the definition of pyemia; septic thrombophlebitis, not phlebothrombosis, is the book's stated origin of the septic emboli that define pyemia.
explanations.D: Correct. The department book defines pyemia as the circulation of septic emboli, originating from septic thrombophlebitis, in the blood; these emboli impact in vessels with a small lumen and form a pyemic abscess. Grossly, a pyemic abscess is multiple, small and yellow, surrounded by a zone of hyperemia related to a blood vessel at the organ's periphery, and microscopically shows a blood vessel with a nearby focus of suppuration surrounded by a pyogenic membrane — the book's own worked types (pulmonary, systemic and portal pyemia) each trace back to septic thrombophlebitis somewhere in the venous circuit feeding that organ.

questions.learning_objective: Define pyemia as circulating septic emboli from septic thrombophlebitis, forming pyemic abscesses, and distinguish it from septicemia and bacteraemia.

questions.title: Most common cause of death in AIDS
questions.question: Most common cause of death in AIDS infected patients is:

options.D: Autoimmune diseases secondary to T-Helper cells dysfunction

explanations.A: Incorrect. Kaposi's sarcoma is one of the malignant neoplasms the book lists as occurring in the final crisis phase of HIV infection, but the book names opportunistic infection, not a specific neoplasm, as the main cause of death.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is likewise one of the AIDS-associated malignancies the book lists, but it is not what the book identifies as the leading cause of death.
explanations.C: Correct. The department book states directly that opportunistic infections are the main cause of death in AIDS, occurring in the final crisis phase once host defence breaks down and viral replication recrudesces. It lists protozoal and helminthic infections (strongyloidiasis, pneumocystis), fungal infections (candidiasis, histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis), bacterial infections (tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteriosis, salmonella and shigella) and viral infections (cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, EBV) as the organisms responsible, reflecting the selective loss of CD4+ helper T cells and impaired function of the surviving ones that HIV, a retrovirus, produces.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The book frames AIDS mortality around opportunistic infection and malignancy arising from the loss of CD4+ T-helper cell function, not around an autoimmune process; it does not describe autoimmune disease as the leading cause of death.

questions.learning_objective: State that opportunistic infection, not a specific neoplasm or autoimmune process, is the main cause of death in AIDS, and name the organism categories involved.

questions.title: Neoplasm seen in AIDS
questions.question: One of the following neoplasms can be seen in AIDS:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Common warts are a benign HPV lesion in the department book's HPV section, not one of the malignant neoplasms the book lists under the AIDS crisis phase.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cancer cervix is discussed in the book under high-risk HPV strains (16 and 18), but it is not among the malignancies the book's own AIDS section names — non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, Burkitt's lymphoma, primary CNS lymphoma and Kaposi's sarcoma — as arising in the final crisis phase of HIV infection.
explanations.C: Correct. The department book lists primary CNS lymphoma, alongside non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, Burkitt's lymphoma and Kaposi's sarcoma, as one of the malignant neoplasms that arise in the final crisis phase of AIDS, once breakdown of host defence lets both opportunistic infection and these tumours emerge. This same crisis-phase malignancy list also includes Kaposi's sarcoma and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, so a question naming any one of these four tumours is drawing on the same book passage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Genital warts (condyloma acuminatum) are a benign, sexually transmitted HPV lesion in the book's HPV section, not a malignant neoplasm, and are not among the book's list of AIDS-associated tumours.

questions.learning_objective: Name primary CNS lymphoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma, Burkitt's lymphoma and Kaposi's sarcoma as the book's AIDS-associated malignancies, and distinguish them from benign HPV lesions.

questions.title: Hepatic bilharziasis
questions.question: Which is true about hepatic bilharziasis:

options.A: The portal tracts may show dilated vascular channels
options.B: At a late stage of the disease the liver appears markedly enlarged
options.C: The hepatic framework is markedly disturbed
options.D: The Kupffer cells engulf bile pigment due to jaundice

explanations.A: Correct. The department book describes angiomatoid formation in the portal tracts of hepatic bilharziasis: dilated, congested anastomotic collateral channels that open between branches of the hepatic artery and portal vein to bypass the fibrotic obstruction of the portal tracts caused by repeated ova emboli. This is one of the book's three named microscopic portal-tract findings, alongside widening by fibrosis and ova surrounded by granulomas, and it is part of the mechanism the book gives for how portal hypertension develops — angiomatoids convey the higher pressure of the hepatic artery directly to the portal veins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The book states the liver is enlarged only early, from reticuloendothelial cell hyperplasia; at a late stage, with progressive portal fibrosis, it becomes shrunken, firm, with an irregular surface and thickened capsule — the reverse of what this option claims.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The book states explicitly that the liver cells and lobules are not affected in hepatic bilharziasis — only the portal tracts (fibrosis, ova granulomas, angiomatoids) and the sinusoids (increased hematin-laden Kupffer cells) are involved, so the hepatic parenchymal framework itself is preserved, not disturbed.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The book attributes the pigment in Kupffer cells to hematin taken up from bilharzial pigment, giving the cut liver surface its dark brown colour, not to bile pigment from jaundice; hepatic bilharziasis in the book's description is a portal fibrosing disease, not a cholestatic one.

questions.learning_objective: Describe hepatic bilharzial periportal fibrosis: preserved liver lobules, portal tract fibrosis and angiomatoid channels, and progression from early enlargement to late shrinkage.

questions.title: Complications of rectal bilharziasis
questions.question: Bilharziasis of the rectum can lead to all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (this is a true complication, not the EXCEPT). The department book lists hemorrhage — fresh blood in the stool, since the lesions sit in the rectosigmoid region — as a complication of bilharzial colitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (this is a true complication, not the EXCEPT). The book states that ova from the colon are carried as emboli through the portal vein to the liver, so hepatic bilharziasis is itself a described route of spread from the colonic infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect (this is a true complication, not the EXCEPT). The book lists secondary infection of the bilharzial ulcers resulting in dysentery — diarrhea, blood, mucus and tenesmus — as a complication of bilharzial colitis.
explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The book's list of complications for bilharziasis of the large intestine covers hemorrhage, secondary infection with dysentery, and (rarely) stenosis and intestinal obstruction; it does not name colon cancer as a complication of colonic bilharziasis. This is unlike the urinary bladder, where the book explicitly names cystitis glandularis and leukoplakia as precancerous lesions predisposing to malignant transformation — a distinction the exam is testing directly.

questions.learning_objective: List the complications of colonic (rectosigmoid) bilharziasis (hemorrhage, dysentery, hepatic spread via the portal vein) and recognise that, unlike bladder bilharziasis, the book does not name colon cancer among them.
